newsitem.title: UK: Forex industry fights back as ACI regroups.
newsitem.headline: Forex industry fights back as ACI regroups.

text.p: As European monetary union, electronic broking and bank mergers threaten to squeeze the life from foreign exchanges, the industry is training new members, seeking out emerging markets and updating its image.

The thorny realities facing delegates at this week's 39th annual gathering of the Association Cambiste Internationale (ACI) in Toronto are not going to go away but the industry can and will adapt, senior professionals say.
The ACI says it can lead the way by encouraging greater recognition of the body by supervisors, developing training programs and expanding membership.
"We are at the turning point of our history. If we don't get the right turn we will disappear," said ACI President Eugene Prim, who presides over his second annual congress at Forex '97.
"We have a shrinking market, not only because of electronic broking," said Prim, who is Senior Manager for International Relations at Kredietbank in Luxembourg.
Monetary union in Europe and the globalization of banks are also forcing the industry to wake up from the heady days of 1992 and 1993.

The ACI, which has about 25,000 individual members in more than 60 countries worldwide, convenes this year for the last time before the founding countries of the new European single currency are announced in spring 1998.

Hand-wringing over the disappearance of up to 10 European currencies on January 1, 1999, has compounded an already steady erosion of traditional forex staffers. Telephone-based broking has suffered a severe blow in recent years as banks favour less labour-intensive electronic trading.
To cap it all, the 1990s heralded consolidation in the banking industry as 'survival of the fittest' took root and mergers between forex giants became the trend.
"With these three things together, we desperately need new markets and new currencies to deal. I think we have a big chance here," Prim said.
Rising interest in emerging currencies was spotlighted this month, with wild movements in the Thai baht and Czech crown.

"The emerging markets are growing in significance and importance to us all and, as an industry, the increased ability to do business in these currencies is pulling people in that direction," said Graham Cocks, vice-president and head of foreign exchange at Bank of Boston in London.
"These are still relatively immature and illiquid, as anyone caught on the wrong side of the Thai baht will testify to, but there are growing opportunities nonetheless."
These new markets have also restored faith in the continued need for trained dealers skilled in telephone dealing and one-on-one contact.

"There is still a need for personal relationships between banks for very specific deals," said the ACI's Prim. "With the explosion of the Czech koruna recently, there was no one offering Czech on dealing systems - you had to pick up the phone."
Moreover, the pessimism about last year's collapse in volatility in major markets is also lifting as volumes and opportunities shift away from the core euro crosses.

Clint Williams, director of foreign exchange recruitment consultant Forex Selection, says he believes the EMU-related staffing retrenchment has run its course anyway and was probably overly aggressive to begin with.
"My own view is that it was well overdone and there is going to be a scramble to re-hire some of the people who were shed."
While the major G7 currencies still retain the lion's share of volumes, the diversity of the market is growing ever wider.
"We also have Africa," Prim said. "It's a huge continent with a financial and foreign exchange market that is underdeveloped."

This spotlights the ACI's growing role as a recognised body for educating new dealers. "There will be more pressure from supervisors around the world to come up with a sort of license to deal. We are close to decisions like that."
"In Zimbabwe the central bank is very keen on developing the financial market and we have about 300 members which have gone already to ACI training."
In London, the world's biggest foreign exchange centre, the need to update and look ahead has also taken hold.
"The EMU issue is one of competitiveness. People have woken up and we realise we've got to do something about it," said Bob Blower, assistant director at the British Bankers Association.
The paranoia about EMU here is also dissipating.
"It would be crass of anyone to say there is no concern about the impact on volumes from EMU but there's no need for anyone to overreact," said Cocks at Bank of Boston.

"As long as the UK stays out of EMU I suspect we could see a contraction of about 10 percent," he said. "While this is significant, it has to be taken in the context of a market that was up about 30 percent in the 1992-to-1995 reporting period."
